title: The kiss and the linen (Mark 14:43–52)
hookLine: betrayed with a kiss; a young man flees naked, a detail only Mark keeps

lines: A CROWD WITH SWORDS AND CLUBS.
cards: He's still speaking to his sleepy friends when Judas arrives, one of the twelve, with a crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent by the chief priests and the scribes and the elders.
Judas has given them a signal, so they take the right man. In the King James Bible: "Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he; take him, and lead him away safely."
Judas walks straight up to Jesus, says, "Master, master," and kisses him. When he plans the signal, Mark's Greek uses the plain word for kiss.
When he does it, Mark uses a longer form, and some readers hear it as warm, the way you'd greet someone you love.

teach.b: They seize him. Someone standing by pulls a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant. Mark doesn't say who; John's Gospel later names Peter.

Jesus speaks to the crowd: have you come out with swords and clubs as if I were a bandit? Day after day I was with you in the temple, teaching, and you didn't arrest me. But let the scriptures be fulfilled.

teach.h: THEY ALL FORSOOK HIM, AND FLED.
teach.b: Then the sentence the whole evening has been leading to: "And they all forsook him, and fled." Earlier that night they all said they'd die with him. Now every one is running through the dark.
Then something strange, which Matthew and Luke leave out. "And there followed him a certain young man, having a linen cloth cast about his naked body."
They grab him, and he wriggles out of the cloth and runs off naked, leaving them holding the linen. Who was he? The text is silent.
An old guess says it was Mark himself, signing his gospel with an embarrassing memory. Some readers hear an echo of the prophet Amos: on that day even the bravest will flee away naked.

teach.h: A YOUNG MAN IN A LINEN CLOTH.
teach.b: Others notice the linen, because a linen cloth will appear again later in this story, and so will a young man.

teach.h: WHO WAS HE? THE TEXT IS SILENT.
teach.b: The picture is clear: one last follower, trying to stay close, leaves everything and runs. Christians have often seen themselves here. Not in the kiss, but in the running.

teach.h: AND THEY ALL FORSOOK HIM, AND FLED.
teach.b: And they notice that the one left alone is the one who does not run.

how: Christians remember the arrest on Maundy Thursday night and Good Friday, and some churches strip the altar bare in silence after the Thursday service as a sign of Jesus left alone.

games.q: you're one of the twelve. swords, clubs, a kiss, and your teacher is seized. earlier tonight you swore you'd die with him. what do you do?
games.why: "they all forsook him, and fled." every one. the last to follow was a young man who ran off, leaving his linen behind.

practice: People flee hard things in different ways: some go silent, some go busy, some scroll, some make a joke, some leave the room.

Without scolding yourself, notice yours the way you'd notice a habit in a friend, and picture the last time you ran and what you left behind in someone else's hands. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God honestly.

wordCard.voice: Amos, the prophet some readers hear echoed here: on that day even the bravest will flee away naked.
